# FDA Completes Almond Risk Assessment, Paves Way for Pasteurization Label

Published 5/10/2017


Updated 6/1/2020


The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently completed its risk assessment of California Almonds, and their conclusions are similar to those made by Almond Board of California (ABC) after conducting its own risk assessments completed in 2006 and 2012 and performed by Linda Harris, Cooperative Extension Specialist in Food Science and Technology, UC Davis and her colleagues. Those risk assessments supported the requirement for a 4-log reduction process under the [mandatory treatment rule](http://www.almonds.com/sites/default/files/content/attachments/pasteurization_federal_register_ruling.pdf), which became effective in 2007.

“FDA’s conclusions are similar to ours as to what level of treatment results in less than one case of salmonellosis per year in the U.S. population,” Dr. Harris said. That level of treatment is the 4-log reduction.

The FDA’s almond risk assessment was triggered by a request from ABC to recognize a 4-log treatment for _Salmonella_ as being equivalent to a pasteurized product, which is normally considered a 5-log reduction. “Currently, almonds treated for 5-log can be labeled “pasteurized,” Dr. Harris said, “but in the almond mandatory _Salmonella_ rule, a 4-log reduction in _Salmonella_ is the standard.”

FDA began collecting data for this risk assessment in 2013, requesting data from the tree nut industry in general, including almonds, precans, pistachios and walnuts. Risk assessments for some of the other tree nuts are expected within a year.

Data supplied to FDA came from ABC and Harris, including some that had not previously been published.

“FDA took the framework of the risk assessment we did in 2012 and did a deep dive into what we had done, added the new data, and took a new look at analyzing the data,” Harris said. “They did a much deeper statistical, mathematical analysis than what we had done.”

One of the largest data packets submitted to FDA is nine years of _Salmonella_ survey data, funded by ABC, consisting of over 15,000 samples. Those data include not only the prevalence of _Salmonella_ in raw California almonds, but also the levels of _Salmonella_ in those positive samples, according to Harris. “The more data the more accurate the risk assessment,” she said, “and having a data set that involves 15,000 samples is a very strong data set.”

FDA’s risk analysis verifies our conclusions and lends support to the 4-log process control target that is in the pasteurization rule, but it doesn’t answer the question about labeling product as “pasteurized.” However, ABC is now in a position to resubmit its request to FDA to consider a 4-log reduction to be pasteurized, using FDA’s own risk-assessment data as rationale.  ABC plans to submit a 4-log process to FDA for consideration in the near future.

# Food Safety

With almonds holding the title as California’s number one agricultural export, it’s never been more important for our industry to be doing everything possible to provide a plentiful, healthful, and safe food product. That’s why the Almond Board of California is 100 percent committed to developing initiatives aimed at topics of concern for both almond producers and consumers.


#### Crunching on the safe side.

California almond farmers grow virtually 100 percent of the United States’ (U.S.) supply of almonds, making the U.S. the single largest market for almonds grown in California. We take great pride in providing a wholesome and safe food for consumers in the U.S. and around the world to enjoy, and that’s why it has never been more important for our industry to be doing everything possible to have a state-of-the-art food safety system in place.

#### A safe and quality product starts in the almond orchard.

From almond growers and handlers to processing, packaging, and sales, our Food Quality and Safety Program is continually evolving to ensure almonds are produced in a safe, responsible manner throughout the food supply chain, so consumers around the world can have the highest level of confidence in our product.

Specifically, the Almond Board regularly educates its growers and handlers on [Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs)](https://www.almonds.com/sites/default/files/2020-04/gap-manual.pdf) in our orchards and [Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs)](https://www.almonds.com/sites/default/files/2020-04/gmp-manual.pdf) in our processing plans.

Our program also includes controls such as environmental monitoring and the pasteurization of almonds before being sold to consumers in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Together, these practices are designed to provide consumers with the safest possible almonds from California.

#### The “raw” deal: facts about almond pasteurization.

Nowadays, almond pasteurization is required by law in the U.S, Canada, and Mexico. We see it as our responsibility to provide a safe, pathogen-free, nutritious food product.

Several years ago after two Salmonella outbreaks traced to California almonds, the California almond community conducted research and learned that there is a low-level presence of Salmonella occurring naturally in the soil across the whole California almond growing region, which resulted in a risk of low-level Salmonella contamination on almonds. We felt it would be irresponsible to have that knowledge and not take an active step to reduce the risk of people getting really sick.

We know that consumers choose almonds for both taste and wellness reasons, and we don't want to change any of the great qualities we all love about almonds. To that end, several pasteurization methods are used that maintain the raw characteristics of almonds--their taste, texture, and nutritional characteristics, including blanching, oil roasting, steaming, and using propylene oxide (PPO). PPO is a compound approved by the U.S. Food & Drug Administration for use to pasteurize food products such as nuts, cocoa powder, and spices.

Products using all of these methods are widely available, and you can always ask the manufacturer of your favorite products which pasteurization method they use.

Our significant investment in research and programs helps maximize quality, consistency, and safety at the orchard level, as well as throughout processing and distribution. What’s more, we’re also looking toward the future by further expanding our efforts, including the addition of rigorous grower self-assessments in pest, irrigation and nutrition management, energy efficiency, and air quality.

#### Almond Board of California Food Safety programs.

- Our [California Almond Stewardship Platform (CASP)](https://www.almonds.org/almond-industry/stewardship-platform) is designed to monitor the industry’s sustainability practices and identify areas for improvement and education.
- Our Food Quality and Safety Program (FQSP) strengthens the commitment to producing almonds in a safe, responsible manner, and provides consumers around the world with the highest level of confidence in our product.
- Our Pasteurization Program addresses safety throughout the system, from growers and handlers to processing, packaging, and sales. As a result of this program, all almonds are pasteurized before being sold to consumers in North America.

# Pasteurization Program

Almonds introduced into commerce in North America are required to be pasteurized using validated processes. Shipment of unpasteurized almonds to markets outside of North America are allowed only if the product is properly labeled as “unpasteurized,” and should be subjected to an appropriate process prior to introduction into commerce.

![Almonds](https://www.almonds.org/sites/default/files/almonds/AL4P6682%20masthead.JPG)

#### Validation and the processes.

All processes used to treat almonds must be validated by an ABC approved Process Authority and approved by ABC’s Technical Expert Review Panel. Validation is a rigorous process in which testing is conducted to demonstrate the ability to destroy microorganisms on almonds. There are several types of validated processes that effectively eliminate potential contamination in almonds without diminishing the product's quality, nutritional value, or sensory qualities (taste and crunch).  Many processes are currently in use including:

**Oil Roasting, Dry Roasting, and Blanching**

Traditional thermal type processes used for roasting (oil/dry) or hot water skin removal (blanching). Appropriate for organic as well as conventional almonds.

**Steam Processing**

Exposure of nut surface to steam for short periods of time.  Steam can be applied at ambient pressure or under vacuum at reduced temperatures.  Appropriate for organic as well as conventional almonds.

**Moist Heat**

Exposure of nuts to a warm and humid environment for short periods of time. Appropriate for organic as well as conventional almonds.

**Propylene Oxide (PPO)**

Exposure of nuts to an EPA approved fumigant treatment that rapidly dissipates after exposure. Appropriate for conventional almonds.

# Steam Pasteurized Almonds: What Buyers Should Know

Almost every almond sold in the United States has been treated to reduce Salmonella risk before it reaches a food manufacturer. Since 2007, USDA rules have required California almonds to go through a validated pasteurization step, and processors meet that requirement in one of two ways: a steam process or a chemical fumigation. **Steam pasteurized almonds** are treated with controlled moist heat rather than propylene oxide gas, which keeps them eligible for organic and clean-label products and free of chemical residue. The method behind a supplier’s [whole almonds](https://www.jssalmonds.com/product/brown-almonds/) affects how the finished kernel can be labeled and sold, which makes it worth understanding before a product goes into development.

## **Why California Almonds Must Be Pasteurized**

The treatment requirement traces back to two Salmonella outbreaks linked to raw almonds, one in Canada in 2001 and one in Oregon in 2004. In response, the Almond Board of California and the USDA introduced a mandatory treatment rule that took effect on September 1, 2007. Every almond grown in California and sold domestically now has to be processed in a way that achieves at least a 4-log reduction in Salmonella, meaning the treatment lowers any bacteria present by a factor of 10,000.

A few shipments fall outside the rule. Almonds sold direct to consumers at farm stands, product bound for export, and kernels shipped to manufacturers who will further process them can move without treatment, though the untreated product has to be labeled accordingly. For almost any brand buying almonds for a domestic food product, treated almonds are the standard, and the real question is which treatment the supplier uses.

## **Steam Pasteurization vs. PPO Fumigation**

The two approved methods reach the same Salmonella reduction by very different means. Steam pasteurization applies saturated steam to the surface of the kernel for a short, controlled interval, raising the temperature enough to kill Salmonella before the almonds are dried and cooled. Propylene oxide fumigation, usually shortened to PPO, seals the almonds in a chamber and exposes them to a gas that settles on and penetrates the surface.

The practical differences matter more than the mechanics:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Factor** | **Steam pasteurization** | **PPO fumigation** |
| Treatment agent | Moist heat | Propylene oxide gas |
| Organic eligibility | Permitted | Not permitted |
| Chemical residue | None | Trace residue possible |
| Export acceptance | Broadly accepted | Restricted in several markets |
| Clean-label fit | Strong | Limited |

PPO carries a commercial drawback beyond the treatment itself. The EPA classifies propylene oxide as a probable human carcinogen, and it is prohibited in the European Union, Canada, and Mexico. A product treated with PPO cannot be certified organic and is closed off from those export markets, whereas a steam-treated kernel keeps both options open.

## **What Steam Treatment Means for Clean-Label and Organic Products**

Steam changes the almond so little that the FDA still considers a steam-treated kernel to meet the definition of raw. A brand can pasteurize by steam and continue to sell the almond as raw or natural, which is not something a chemical fumigant allows. For clean-label positioning, where the ingredient statement is expected to read short and recognizable, the absence of any chemical treatment is a genuine advantage.

Organic products have no choice in the matter. PPO is not permitted on organic almonds, so any brand building a certified organic line needs a steam-pasteurized supply from the start. The same applies to export programs aimed at Europe or Canada, where PPO-treated product cannot enter. Choosing steam early keeps a formulation eligible for organic certification and international distribution without a disruptive supplier change later.

## **How Steam Pasteurization Affects Flavor and Quality**

Steam pasteurization has minimal impact on the almond when the process is properly controlled. Color, flavor, and nutritional content are preserved, so the kernel blanches, slices, roasts, and grinds just as an untreated almond would, and the oil content that carries flavor into butters and pastes remains intact.

The primary concern is excess heat. When steam is applied for too long or at too high a temperature, it begins to cook the kernel, darkening the color and wrinkling the skin. Running the treatment at a validated time and temperature prevents this, achieving the required Salmonella reduction while preserving the quality of the almond.

## **Sourcing Steam Pasteurized Almonds**

The treatment method is a sourcing decision as much as a food-safety one, because it sets what a brand can claim on the label and where the product can be sold. A supplier that runs a validated steam process, and can produce the documentation behind it, gives a brand room to pursue organic certification, clean-label positioning, and export markets without reworking its supply later.

At JSS Almonds, we supply steam-pasteurized almonds backed by BRCGS AA+ certification, one of the highest food-safety ratings in the industry, along with HACCP controls and environmental monitoring behind every lot. Our almonds come from more than 15,000 acres of California owner-partner orchards, which keeps supply steady and pricing clear of import tariffs. Because we run small minimum order quantities, a brand piloting a short run and one ordering by the pallet both draw from the same certified supply, whether the product calls for whole kernels, [in-shell almonds](https://www.jssalmonds.com/product/in-shell-almonds/), or a broader mix of [wholesale nuts](https://www.jssalmonds.com/product/wholesale-nuts/).

## **Building an Almond Supply You Can Count On**

How an almond is treated decides more than its safety record. It sets whether the kernel can carry a raw or organic claim, clear customs into Europe, and hold a clean ingredient statement, which is why the treatment method belongs in the sourcing conversation from the beginning. JSS Almonds pairs a validated steam-pasteurized supply with the responsiveness a growing brand needs, from first sample through full production, across whole almonds, wholesale nuts, and custom [nut butters](https://www.jssalmonds.com/product/nut-butters/). [Contact our team](https://www.jssalmonds.com/contact/) with the product you are building, and we will match the almond, the treatment, and the documentation to where you plan to sell it.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**

### **Are steam pasteurized almonds still considered raw?**

Yes. The FDA considers steam pasteurization to leave the almond’s essential characteristics unchanged, so a steam-treated kernel can still be labeled and sold as raw or natural. This is not the case for almonds treated with a chemical fumigant.

### **What is the difference between steam pasteurization and PPO?**

Steam pasteurization uses controlled moist heat to reduce Salmonella, while PPO uses propylene oxide gas. Steam leaves no chemical residue and is permitted on organic almonds. PPO is a probable human carcinogen, cannot be used on organic product, and is restricted in the European Union, Canada, and Mexico.

### **Do all California almonds have to be pasteurized?**

Almonds grown in California and sold within the United States must be treated to achieve at least a 4-log reduction in Salmonella under a rule that took effect in 2007. Exemptions apply to direct-to-consumer sales, exports, and almonds shipped for further processing, all of which must be labeled as untreated.

### **Does steam pasteurization change the taste of almonds?**

When the process is properly controlled, steam has little effect on flavor, color, or nutrition. Excessive steam can wrinkle and darken the kernel, which is why a validated process runs to a tested time and temperature that reduces Salmonella without cooking the almond.

### **Can I get organic steam pasteurized almonds?**

Yes. Steam is the only treatment permitted on certified organic almonds, since propylene oxide is prohibited on organic product. A brand building an organic line needs a steam-pasteurized supply to keep its certification intact.
